report.source_text: A CT and MRI of the brain were obtained, which showed a gradient of hyperintense content of the lesion with surrounding relatively hyperintense perilesional edema (Figure 1). The unenhanced CT scan of the brain showed a well-defined iso- to hyper-dense lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema within the right parietal lobe, causing mild mass effect upon the adjacent sulci and posterior horn of the right lateral ventricle. However, there was no midline shift, hydrocephalus, or brain herniation. On the T2-weighted MRI images, the lesion exhibited a fluid-fluid level with predominantly hypointense content. On the other hand, the non-contrast T1-weighted images displayed a gradient of hyperintense content of the lesion with surrounding relatively hyperintense perilesional edema. The most inferior aspect of the lesion exhibited hyperintense content with a rim of hypointensity, featuring a popcorn appearance (Figure 1).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 35-year-old female with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with a 7-day history of progressive left-sided weakness beginning in the upper limb and progressing to the lower limb, accompanied by gait disturbance, falls, and nausea. On examination, she had left-sided weakness (4/5), normal right-sided strength (5/5), normal tone, and bilateral Hoffmann's sign, with intact cognition, language, and attention. Neuroimaging (CT and MRI brain) revealed a right parietal lobe lesion with characteristic cavernoma features: popcorn appearance with hemosiderin rim, fluid-fluid level on T2-weighted imaging (indicating recent hemorrhage), hyperintense gradient on T1-weighted imaging, susceptibility effect on susceptibility-weighted images, thin rim enhancement on post-contrast imaging, and surrounding vasogenic edema with mild mass effect. The radiological constellation of findings was most consistent with a cavernoma. The patient underwent right parietal craniotomy for evacuation of the subacute hematoma and excision of the lesion. Intraoperatively, a subacute hematoma with a mulberry-looking lesion was identified and resected. Post-operatively, the patient was awake, alert, communicating, and stable, and was discharged on post-operative day 5. At six-month follow-up, the patient was doing well with improvement in weakness and minimal post-operative discomfort at the surgical site.
